concept.name: Contract size
concept.definition: The actual quantity of the underlying asset represented by one futures or derivative contract, as standardized by the exchange in the contract specification.
concept.intuition: One 'contract' is a fixed bundle — contract size tells you how big the bundle is, so one futures contract on crude oil always means the same number of barrels.
concept.mechanics: The exchange sets the contract size (e.g., 1,000 barrels for WTI crude futures) so that every contract is fungible. Position exposure equals number of contracts x contract size, and delivery obligations are stated in multiples of the contract size.
concept.formula: Exposure (units of underlying) = N x CS, where N = number of contracts and CS = contract size; dollar notional = N x CS x price for unit-quoted contracts.
concept.failure_modes: Hedgers whose actual exposure is not a multiple of the contract size are left with partial (basis) exposure; mini/micro variants exist partly because the standard size is too coarse for smaller exposures.
concept.misconceptions: Contract size is sometimes confused with margin: the full value controlled by a contract is price x contract size, while margin is only the small good-faith deposit posted against it.
concept.example: One CME WTI crude oil futures contract represents 1,000 barrels, so a trader long 3 contracts controls 3,000 barrels of exposure; if price rises $1 per barrel, the position gains $3,000.
